name: Kira Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Kira, 43, and I operate an electric shovel at the large mine. I start with the bucket teeth and cable check, then load trucks until the rock face changes; I like knowing how to feed a truck cleanly without making the driver wait. The worst part is a wet seam that sticks to the bucket and ruins the schedule. I have a vocational certificate, my partner Owen sells building supplies, and our two children are in school while we pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I already use AI to sort my shift notes, and the shovel still needs an operator. The tool saves me five minutes at handover, but I check every load count myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quiet AI future would suit my work, yet our household is stretched before any new software arrives. My partner Owen sells building supplies on commission, and a slow month plus our mortgage can empty our small reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating the shovel and continue checking my AI draft against the machine log after each shift. In the first year I'd put the commission from Owen's next strong month into the mortgage buffer, before we buy another garden set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fine about the software and restless about the account balance. I like trying a tool early, but enthusiasm does not cover a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the note tool get wrong last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It counted a cancelled load as delivered because I had typed the stop in the wrong column. I corrected the handover before the next crew came in, which is why I never send the draft untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a weak commission month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We leave the garden fence another season and buy school lunches as usual. The children should not have to calculate Owen's sales at breakfast.

say: I would say **AI notes** save time while I still operate the shovel.
I would stress **checking load counts** before handover.
think: I welcome a quiet AI future but worry about **commission income**.
I know our **small reserve** could vanish after a slow month.
do: Keep operating the **shovel** and check each AI handover draft.
Put a strong **sales commission** into the mortgage buffer.
feel: **Confident** with the tool, restless about household cash.
S0.quote: I like trying a tool early, but enthusiasm does not cover a mortgage payment.
fieldNote: Kira uses **AI daily** for notes while verifying it against the machine log.
The **mortgage** and Owen’s variable commission create a money worry independent of technological change.

steps.text: Keep operating the shovel and check AI drafts against machine logs
Put Owen’s next strong commission into the mortgage buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew the planning office will probably shrink first, because the card names the very tasks they do. I would ask to trial the new dispatch board with operators before management sets harder load targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still have a cab, but a cleaner schedule might mean fewer paid standby hours for me. Owen's building-supply orders might also move online, and I cannot predict whether that improves or cuts his commission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the dispatch trial next month and keep a record of delays the software misses. During the first year, if standby hours disappear, I'd take the Saturday equipment-check shift when offered and stop the monthly streaming bundle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested enough to put my name on the trial sheet. I am also worried about being rewarded for speed with a smaller wage packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which delay would the software miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wet seam makes the shovel bucket stick, so the planned loading time is useless for an hour. I want an operator beside the engineer when they decide whether the board is accurate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Owen to change his work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a guess. I'd ask my partner Owen to track online orders against his commission for three months, then we'd decide whether he needs another sales patch.

say: I would say the **planning office** changes before shovel operation.
I would ask for an **operator trial** before tougher targets.
think: I worry fewer **standby hours** would shrink my pay.
I cannot yet tell how online orders affect Owen’s **commission**.
do: Volunteer for the **dispatch trial** and log missed delays.
Take **Saturday checks** if standby hours vanish.
Cancel the **streaming bundle** if wages fall.
feel: **Interested** in the trial and worried about pay.
S1.quote: I am also worried about being rewarded for speed with a smaller wage packet.
fieldNote: Kira wants to **test dispatch** with operator knowledge of wet-seam delays.
Her willingness to try technology sits beside a concrete fear of **lost standby pay** and uncertain commission.

steps.text: Volunteer for dispatch trial and log wet-seam delays
Take Saturday equipment-check shifts if standby hours vanish
Cancel monthly streaming bundle if wages fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 could replace most mine planning, then hands-on robots might take shovels around 2031. I would ask for the robot procurement timetable now, so operators can bid for new work before the seats disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am willing to learn, but I expect the mine to remove many operator shifts once robots can dig as well as we do. At 48 in 2031 I'd still have school-age children and a mortgage, and fewer than one month's expenses cannot fund a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a meeting with the maintenance supervisor this month about sensor and inspection work, then enrol in a paid controls course if the mine opens one. In 2029 I'd apply for a posted equipment-monitoring role and keep driving the shovel while they decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The short clock makes me frightened about income, not about touching new equipment. I would be awake counting how many paydays fit between a redundancy notice and the mortgage debit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the controls course were unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the mine can put it on paid shifts; I cannot finance time off with our current reserve. I might learn a free module at home, but that alone would not qualify me for the monitoring role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Owen do in that case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Owen could cover groceries in a good sales month, but not the mortgage reliably. I would not ask the children to leave their school until I had a real job offer elsewhere.

say: I would name **2028 planning AI** and shovel robots around 2031 separately.
I would ask for a **procurement timetable** before operator seats disappear.
think: I expect **operator shifts** to fall sharply when robots dig.
Our **thin reserve** cannot fund a long search.
do: Meet the **maintenance supervisor** about sensor work.
Enrol in a **paid controls course** if opened.
Apply for a **monitoring role** in 2029 if posted.
feel: **Frightened** by the income clock, not by learning equipment.
S2.quote: I would be awake counting how many paydays fit between a redundancy notice and the mortgage debit.
fieldNote: Kira’s **technical curiosity** does not erase likely income loss when shovel robots arrive.
Her plan relies on **paid training** and a posted role, neither of which she assumes will exist.

steps.text: Meet maintenance supervisor about sensor and inspection work
Enrol in paid controls course if the mine opens one
Apply for posted equipment-monitoring role in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI in 2031 gives us time to test the mine's systems, while shovel robots may follow around 2034. The owners could offer apprenticeships in machine repair to people who know what bad rock does to a bucket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra three years before thinking AI and then three more before robots would let me build a work record in controls. I still cannot assume the mine will need as many monitors as it has shovel drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a free evening controls module this winter and ask the safety lead to let me shadow one sensor inspection each month. In 2032, the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd apply for the mine's controls apprenticeship if paid and continue shovel shifts until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more capable with several years to show what I can do. The mismatch between the number of drivers and possible new posts still makes me anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would an evening module fit family life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen can handle Tuesday supper and the children's reading while I study for an hour. My mother could help some weeks, but I do not want a plan that depends on her every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove you can do controls work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A supervisor seeing me trace a faulty sensor safely would count more than a certificate alone. I would ask for the inspection log to show my name and the fault I found.

say: I would support **repair apprenticeships** for current shovel operators.
I would distinguish **2031 AI** from robots around 2034.
think: I could build a **controls record** before the robots arrive.
I doubt monitoring posts will equal the number of **drivers**.
do: Take a free **evening controls module** this winter.
Apply for a **paid controls apprenticeship** in 2032 if offered.
feel: **Capable**, yet anxious about competition for fewer posts.
S3.quote: A supervisor seeing me trace a faulty sensor safely would count more than a certificate alone.
fieldNote: Kira uses the longer runway to seek **documented inspection experience**, not just classroom knowledge.
Her **apprenticeship application** remains conditional on a paid opening, and she expects competition.

steps.text: Take free evening controls module this winter
Ask safety lead to shadow monthly sensor inspections
Apply for paid controls apprenticeship in 2032 if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years to thinking AI and shovel robots around 2039 is a useful warning, not a reason to coast. I would ask the mine to keep experienced operators involved when it chooses which machines to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when full thinking AI arrives and 56 when shovel robots appear. Our children should be grown then, but I may still owe on the mortgage and I have no pension number to justify stopping work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shovel job and request a pension statement this year instead of guessing at retirement. I'd pay an extra amount toward mortgage principal in strong commission months, and in 2037 I'd check actual controls vacancies before deciding whether to leave the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more room to make choices, although I do not know what the mine will look like in 2039. I would rather prepare while wages come in than wait for a farewell speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave the cab before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written controls offer with reliable pay, or a steady inspection role at another nearby mine. I would not trade this wage for a course advert, even though I like learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your children figure into the ten-year calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They will be adults, so I won't pretend we're still paying for school lunches. I hope they visit for dinner, and I hope neither needs us to cover their rent.

say: I would use the **ten-year warning** and include operators in automation choices.
I would place shovel robots around **2039**, after thinking AI.
think: I may still need **regular mortgage wages** at 56.
I cannot infer retirement from an unknown **pension amount**.
do: Pay extra **mortgage principal** in strong commission months.
Check **controls vacancies** in 2037 before leaving the cab.
feel: **Room to choose**, with uncertainty about the mine’s future.
S4.quote: I would rather prepare while wages come in than wait for a farewell speech.
fieldNote: Kira does not treat **grown children** as continuing school-age expenses in 2039.
Her long plan combines **mortgage reduction** with a real vacancy check, without assuming pension security.

steps.text: Request an actual pension statement from the mine this year
Pay extra mortgage principal in strong commission months
Apply for a controls vacancy in 2037 if reliable pay is offered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robot shovels around 2031 leave little time to qualify for another paid role. A published procurement timetable and paid controls training tied to real inspection vacancies would help. I am ready to learn, but I cannot learn on wages that disappear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets access to the fault logs while systems are tested. If only engineers see them, operators lose the chance to prove what we notice at the rock face.

headlineQuote: I am ready to learn, but I cannot learn on wages that disappear.
portrait: Kira is a **43-year-old shovel operator** with two school-age children, a mortgage and under one month saved.
She uses **AI daily** for notes but checks the machine log before handing work over.
She expects **planning AI** before shovel robots and seeks practical sensor experience.
She would take **paid controls training** and apply for real roles while keeping income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before robot shovels may reach the mine around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **procurement timetable** and paid controls training tied to inspection vacancies would help Kira.
